name: Aisha Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-fix trainee with Linden Interiors on a block of riverside apartments, 120 flats. Second fix is the finishing carpentry once the walls are plastered: hanging doors, fitting kitchens, skirting, architrave, door handles and locks. I'm still slow and my mitres aren't always tight, so Corinne (my supervisor) checks every flat before the client walks it. I really like the finish work, when a kitchen goes in and suddenly it looks like somebody's home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's your setup?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Noor, and I've got about four months of expenses saved. I left school early and came to building at twenty-four after shop work. I'm on AI all day, honestly: I photograph awkward details and ask how to fix them, it makes my cutting lists, and it's helping me study for a site supervisor's certificate in the evenings. My plan was always to end up running sites, not swinging a hammer at fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not the miracle people said. I'd probably post something like that, half joking. At work nobody would care much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes. Linden has fit-out work booked into 2028 and there's loads of apartment building round the river. I'd keep learning, and keep using it for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the supervisor certificate by next June. I'd ask Corinne to let me shadow her on handovers. And I'd keep doing a couple of weekend kitchen fits for friends of friends for extra cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Like the plan still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, just the normal stuff. Fit-out work stops dead if the developer runs out of money, and that happened to a firm my mate worked for. But Linden's been solid for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your evening studying, does that still make sense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. Running a site still needs a person who can stand in a muddy corridor and tell a plumber no. The certificate is my way up.

say: I'd say AI is **still useful**, just not a miracle.
I'd post it **half joking**, and nobody at work would care much.
think: Linden has **fit-out work** booked into 2028, so little changes.
I'd keep using AI for the **boring bits** of the job.
do: Finish the **site supervisor certificate** by next June.
Shadow Corinne on **handovers** to the client.
Keep doing **weekend kitchen fits** for extra cash.
feel: She feels **calm**, like the plan still works.
S0.quote: Running a site still needs a person who can stand in a muddy corridor and tell a plumber no.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **all day** as a junior, unusual on site.
Her ladder is from fitting to **running sites**, a thinking role.
Her only background worry is a **developer going bust**.

steps.text: Finish the site supervisor certificate by next June
Shadow Corinne (her supervisor) on client handovers
Keep doing weekend kitchen fits for friends of friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn to use it or get left behind, which is easy for me to say. I'd probably share tips with the other trainees on our group chat. I'd be careful not to sound smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one gets me. Planning, ordering, checking, programmes: that's exactly what a site manager does, and that's where I was heading. The fitting is the safe bit now, which is the opposite of what I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the certificate going but change the aim to supervising people and quality on site, the walk-round part, not the spreadsheets. I'd get properly good at fitting kitchens, because that's the hands-on skill. I'd also learn whatever planning software Linden brings in better than anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like finding out the road you're on bends somewhere you didn't expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your plan is to run sites. Does that still look like the right move here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I spent a year studying to do the office half of a site manager's job, and that's the half the software takes first. So maybe it's still right, just a different version of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Corinne about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask her what she actually spends her day doing. If it's mostly on the phone and the laptop, I'd tell her honestly that it's coming for that bit. She'd probably laugh and say she's been saying the same for a year.

say: I'd say **learn to use it** or get left behind.
I'd share **AI tips** with other trainees, careful not to sound smug.
think: Planning and ordering, the **site manager's desk work**, is where I was heading.
The **fitting** is now the safer half, which surprises me.
do: Refocus the certificate on **supervising people** and quality walk-rounds.
Get properly good at **fitting kitchens** by hand.
Learn Linden's **planning software** better than anyone.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, like the road bends somewhere unexpected.
S1.quote: I spent a year studying to do the office half of a site manager's job, and that's the half the software takes first.
fieldNote: Her planned **escape route** into management is the part AI hits first.
She adjusts quickly, shifting her aim to **people and quality**.
She sees fitting as **safer** than she thought.

steps.text: Refocus the supervisor course on quality walk-rounds and people
Practise kitchen fitting until she can do one unchecked
Learn Linden's planning software better than anyone on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone needs to move now, and the government should help people get there. I'd post practical stuff, like which courses are worth it. I wouldn't panic people, but I wouldn't pretend either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 the office side of site management is gone, so my certificate is mostly worthless. Then by 2031 robots can hang doors and fit kitchens. I'd be thirty-two with a plan that died twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the supervisor course and put that time into learning to run and set up the robots that'll come for fit-out. I'd ask Linden to put me on any trial. I'd stop the weekend kitchens if they paid nothing, and save harder, maybe six months by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit buzzing too. Scary, but I'd rather be in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between 2028 and 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to become the person who works the machines instead of the person they replace. The robots arrive in 2031, so the window to stop being a fitter and become a robot operator is about three years. If I'm fast, it's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut from your spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, the gym, the holiday to see my cousins. I'd keep the phone and laptop, because those are how I'd learn.

say: I'd say everyone needs to **move now**, with government help.
I'd post **practical advice** on which courses are worth doing.
think: By **2028** the office side of site management is gone.
By **2031** robots can hang doors and fit kitchens.
do: Drop the supervisor course and learn to **operate fit-out robots**.
Ask Linden to put her on any **robot trial**.
Save toward **six months** of expenses by 2030.
feel: She feels **anxious**, but a bit **buzzing** too.
S2.quote: The robots arrive in 2031, so the window to stop being a fitter and become a robot operator is about three years.
fieldNote: Her plan **dies twice**: once in 2028, then again in 2031.
She treats the **three-year gap** as a concrete window to switch.
Her adaptability turns fear into a wish to be **in the middle** of change.

steps.text: Drop the supervisor course and study robot operation instead
Ask Linden to put her on any fit-out robot trial
Cut eating out, gym and holiday to reach six months' savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get it right. I'd tell people to pick something they're interested in and start now. Probably share a few course links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. I'd have the certificate and a couple of years supervising by 2031, then three years to learn the robot side before 2034. I think I'd come out of it OK, maybe better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate, then aim for a quality and handover role, the person who walks a flat and decides if it's done. I'd learn the planning software in my own time. And I'd keep the weekend kitchens going for extra savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly fine. Like there's a bridge, I just need to cross it at the right time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years bring the supervisor plan back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. Five years turns my supervisor certificate from a dead end into a stepping stone, as long as I don't stand on it too long. I'd use it, then move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's a nurse, so she'd laugh at me worrying. I'd tell her I'm fine, but I need to keep moving. She'd probably say I always am.

say: I'd say there's **time** to get it **right**.
I'd tell people to **pick something** they like and start now.
think: I'd have the **certificate** and some supervising by 2031.
Three more years to learn the **robot side** before 2034.
do: Finish the certificate and aim for a **quality and handover** role.
Learn the **planning software** in her own time.
Keep **weekend kitchens** going for extra savings.
feel: She feels **uneasy but mostly fine**, with a bridge to cross.
S3.quote: Five years turns my supervisor certificate from a dead end into a stepping stone, as long as I don't stand on it too long.
fieldNote: Five years turns her certificate into a **stepping stone**.
Her target shifts to **quality and handover**, where human judgement stays.
Living with a nurse, she has a **steady flatmate** sharing rent.

steps.text: Finish the certificate and apply for a quality and handover role
Learn the planning software in her own time
Keep weekend kitchen fits going to grow savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent warning and people should use it. I'd be pretty relaxed about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough to run a site and then move into managing the machines that do the work. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when the robots land. That's a good age to be the experienced one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing much: finish the certificate, keep fitting, keep the weekend work. In a few years I'd move up to supervising, and maybe learn robotics part time once there's a decent course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 2036 look like for you, if it goes well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By thirty-seven I want to be the one who signs off a building that robots fitted out, because I know what a good door looks like. Good pay, a flat I own, maybe a small fit-out firm with Corinne.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could trip you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfy. If things are going well, it's easy to stop learning. And the developer going bust, which never goes away.

say: I'd say ten years is a **decent warning**.
I'd tell people to **use the time** and stay relaxed.
think: Ten years is enough to **run a site**, then manage machines.
Being forty when robots land makes me **the experienced one**.
do: Finish the certificate and keep **weekend work** going.
Move up to **supervising** in a few years.
Learn **robotics part time** once a decent course exists.
feel: She feels **calm**, with a long runway.
S4.quote: By thirty-seven I want to be the one who signs off a building that robots fitted out, because I know what a good door looks like.
fieldNote: The long timeline brings back her **original ambition**.
She sees **experience** as her edge when robots land.
Her ongoing worry is complacency and **developer failure**.

steps.text: Move up to supervising fit-out within a few years
Learn robotics part time once a decent course exists
Keep weekend kitchen fits going for extra income

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because it kills my plan twice in three years. Everyone told me to get off the tools and into the office, and the office is exactly where AI arrives first. What would help is a proper course on running site robots that I could start now, not in five years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me are already doing. I'm a trainee and I use AI more than my bosses do. Nobody asks us juniors how the tools could be used, but we're the ones trying them.

headlineQuote: Everyone told me to get off the tools and into the office, and the office is exactly where AI arrives first.
portrait: Aisha is a 27-year-old **second-fix trainee** on a riverside apartment fit-out.
She shares a flat with **Noor**, a nurse, and has about **four months** saved.
She uses AI **all day** and was studying to become a site supervisor.
She realises the **office half** of site management is most exposed, and adjusts her plan.
She's **anxious** with two years' warning but calm with ten, seeing experience as her edge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which kills her management plan in 2028 and her fitting work by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A proper course on **running site robots** she could start now.
